speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite continuing over-all balance of payments problems which have plagued Canada throughout the years of office of the Liberal Government, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has of late, in order to focus attention on some small bright spot in the economy, made frequent reference to recent merchandise trade balance figures which have been in Canada's favour. However, even in this traditionally favourable area we can see significant deterioration as a result of Liberal trade policy.
The February figures show a decline in external trade surplus of a billion dollars since January. The $2.1 billion January surplus has been reduced to $1.1 billion in February, surely a most alarming trend which, unless reversed, will result in further pressure on the Canadian dollar and, subsequently, higher domestic rates. We cannot allow Canada's financial relationships to worsen. Government policy has to be changed to encourage an inflow of funds into our country rather than the outflow seemingly favoured by the Liberals.

subsubtopic: FUEL AND LOAN COSTS OF FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Manitoba farmers can expect little relief from the Government. This week the Farm Credit Corporation increased its lending rate to 15 per cent for long-term loans. At the same time the Government introduced Bill C-14 which will cut the effective rate of tax at the wellhead to 11 per cent for the oil companies, yet the Government continues to refuse to follow the lead of the Manitoba Government and eliminate sales tax on farm fuels.
In 1981 Manitoba farmers used 415 million litres of petroleum fuels in their operations that cost them the tidy sum of $124 million, of which $12 million was federal sales tax. I
cannot understand why the Government continues to be so willing to give tax breaks to the major oil companies yet still refuses to give just a little relief to farmers.
[DOT] (mo)
It is not surprising that farm bankruptcies have increased by a staggering 58 per cent in the first months of 1984. This is supposed to be a year of recovery, but it is very clear that that recovery is not touching farmers. Instead of being an agency that is helping farmers weather these tough times, the Farm Credit Corporation seems to be doing all it can to make life more difficult for them.
I related an example of this the other day in the House when I told the story of a couple of young farmers who live in my constituency. They went to the Farm Credit Corporation looking for help to meet their loan payments, and were rebuffed. I call upon the Government of the country to do more for farmers, and to save the family farm in Canada.

subsubtopic: POLLUTION DANGER TO NIAGARA RIVER-UNITED STATES COURT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's Minister of the Environment (Mr. Caccia) pondered and stalled during the time allowed by United States District Court Judge Curtin for Canadian intervention on the proposed Niagara S-Area cleanup settlement between Occidental Chemical Corporation and the United States Government. That time has now expired and, except for the Province of Ontario, the court offers only friend of the court status to others, limiting the opportunity to present and challenge evidence, to appeal the court decision, or to monitor conditions of settlement.
Environment Canada's consultants have determined that the proposed settlement is unsatisfactory. Canadian environment officials say that there are no guarantees that the containment program will do the job necessary to protect Canadian interests in the Niagara River. Too late the Minister cries foul, and says that he will once more ask the United States Government to withdraw from the cleanup plan and get on with the removal of the S-Area chemical dump.
There has been enough talk, Mr. Speaker. The Government of Canada can become involved, if not directly then by actively assisting the citizens' groups which propose to file a lawsuit, if they have not yet done so, against Occidental Chemical for alleged environmental damage created by that dump site.

subtopic: S O. 21 INDUSTRY INCREASED PRODUCTIVITY IN MANUFACTURING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to counter the negative and false statements made by the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) by drawing to the attention of the House a Statistics Canada report released last week which stated that, in 1983, Canadian manufacturing employees produced more for every hour worked than they have since 1971. In fact they out-performed all of our competitors. We also discovered last week that productivity in manufacturing increased by 6.9 per cent last year, and in the commercial sector it increased by 3.3 per cent.
By increasing productivity growth we have conquered one of the major economic maladies afflicting the country. This peak in Canadian productivity is reason enough for the government, and indeed for all Canadians, to smile. Among other positive benefits, productivity growth improves Canada's competitive position in international markets, is a key factor in determining the growth in our standard of living, and will give us strength in continuing to fight inflation.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has said: "Past performance and past spending habits will not sustain us in a fiercely competitive international marketplace. We must become better than the competition-better at producing and marketing goods and services-and better at working together for the shared economic interests of all Canadians". It is my firm conviction that the Government's economic program of action is definitely one which is leading Canadians from recovery to expansion.

speechtext:

On the use of government aircraft, the guidelines are written, but they were written for ministerial conduct generally, whether they are on leadership business or not.

Not only is the Government building a very prestigious edifice in honour of and at the time of the Fair, but also I have personally, in my correspondence with leaders of other Governments, and in my travels, talked about the Fair and in many cases exercised some subtle pressure to get other countries to participate in the fair. In that sense, without having followed the file very closely, I can only commend Premier Bennett for making sure that cost overruns are held to a minimum. subtopic: SALE OF PLANT-REQUEST FOR GUARANTEES OF FUTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister just said that the plant in question is to be sold to National Sea Products Limited for $1, despite the fact that the plant will be worth approximately $5 million after the Government itself invests $2.3 million into upgrading that plant.
Oral Questions
In light of what he has just said, would the Minister tell us what guarantees the federal Government has obtained from National Sea Products in case that parent company gets into financial difficulty and is no longer able to operate the plant? What guarantees has it been able to get from the company to ensure that the assets of the plant and the fish allocation associated with it revert to Prince Edward Island and to Georgetown, rather than being absorbed into any financial difficulties, even bankruptcy, that the company concerned might incur?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre De Bane (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: SALE OF PLANT-REQUEST FOR GUARANTEES OF FUTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we cannot have it both ways. There is nobody in Canada whose job is guaranteed. What the federal Government has done is go to the limit of investing whatever money is needed to restructure that company along the wishes of the private sector. When you ask me what guarantee there is that the company will never fail, I frankly ask how the Hon. Member can put a question like that.
Every day, thousands of companies go under, and thousands of new ones are formed. All I can hope is that the private sector which has taken control of the company and has shown confidence by investing up to $20 million, will prove to be good managers. The federal Government, as the Hon. Member would admit, has gone to the extreme limit of allowing the private sector to show their capabilities. Of course I cannot guarantee to anyone in Canada, whether in the public or private sector, that they do not have to compete in this very competitive world.

subsubtopic: DEPORTATION OF SIKHS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Federation of Sikh Societies of Canada is concerned that there are Sikhs under refugee status in Canada who are daily being deported. In the absence of the Minister of Employment and Immigration I will direct my question to the Prime Minister. It concerns the Sikhs who are daily being deported at this time to Punjab, India.
Is the Prime Minister aware that the new National Security Act in India may mean that these deported refugees could be jailed without trial? Would he consider asking his Minister to hold these deportation orders in abeyance until something could be negotiated with the Federation of Sikh Societies of Canada, which is the national body of Sikhs, to enable these refugees to remain in Canada? In other words, would the Prime Minister undertake to ask his Minister of Employment and Immigration to hold discussions with the Federation on this important matter?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES ON RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Prime Minister. As Dr. Kerwin, President of the National Research Council, has stated: "Each additional one per cent of Gross National Product that is spent on research and development will produce 800,000 new jobs". Since the federal Government's share of the national expenditure on research and development has fallen from 48 per cent in 1968 to 37 per cent today, will the Prime Minister advise the House why the federal Government has cut back its share, instead of giving leadership in increasing research and development and thereby providing the additional jobs which Canadians need so badly today?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES ON RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I begged the Hon. Member the last time when we talked about research and development to check the facts. He has and, I might have known, he checked two sets of facts and confused them. First he says that our share has fallen, which is true, and then he says that we have cut back. It does not follow that because our share has fallen we have cut back. What could very well follow is that the other participants in research and
development have decided to spend more, in other words, have followed the example of the federal Government.
The Hon. Member will remember that in our previous exchanges I said he was confused because he was talking about research and development as a global matter and blaming us for not doing enough. I said he should look-which he did, and I am glad he took my advice; he should do so more often-at the shares of the other participants and should realize that they have not been doing, in comparison with the private sector in other countries, and even with the academic sector in other countries, as well as they might. They heeded my advice. They are now spending more. They are spending a more reasonable share of the total. That is what is happening, and 1 am sure the Hon. Member will understand it if he spends the weekend on the problem.

That whereas the economic problems facing Canadian farmers today are largely the result of Government inaction and neglect, this House condemns the Government for its failure to recognize the importance of the agricultural sector and its contribution to economic growth in Canada and urges the Government to move quickly to reduce the farm fuel tax, introduce a red meat stabilization plan, expedite the passage of legislation respecting advance payments, resist the erosion of initial payments for Western grain, pass urgently needed amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act, and reduce high interest rates and take steps to facilitate the introduction of agri-bonds.
He said: Mr. Speaker, agriculture has had some exposure in the House this week, and justifiably so. There was an NDP opposition motion on Wednesday and some questions today on agriculture. It is an important topic for this country. Too often many of us simply take agriculture for granted. One reason that happens is that farmers basically are very efficient. As they become more efficient, there are fewer farmers and, therefore, less political influence and political clout. Nevertheless it is a subject that is extremely important.
I will put a couple of figures on the record. This has been done many times by those of us who speak on this topic. Agriculture accounts for 20 per cent of the employment in this country. In addition, it is a very substantial earner of foreign exchange. I suspect that Canadian agricultural exports in the past year will amount to close to $10 billion, a lot of money. Although the figures are not yet available, if you look at 1982 and what has happened in 1983, I believe $10 billion is a conservative estimate of the amount of exports for which agriculture was responsible. One way to illustrate what $1 billion represents is to point out that $1 billion amounts to $400 per capita. If agriculture was responsible for exports of $10 billion, that represents $400 for each person in this country. It certainly helps the over-all economy of this country.
As farmers have become more efficient, in the last three or four years they have been farming away some of their equity. If you look at the figures for 1983 over 1982 you see that in
1982	on average-you have to be careful when talking averages because there are wide variances-approximately 16.2 per cent of disposable income was used to feed Canadians. In
1983	the figure went down to under 16 per cent.
Farmers can take some pride in their efficiency. However, it is well known that farmers have been losing money. There have been record bankruptices in this country, not only in the economy in general, but agriculture in particular. One reason they have been able to feed consumers in this country for a smaller percentage of their disposable income is that every time farmers sell what they produce, they sell off some of their equity, some of the value they have in their farm. This cannot continue if we are to maintain a healthy agricultural industry.
April 13, 1984

There are other ways to make the same point. The percentage of the consumer dollar that is spent on food which goes back to the farmer is decreasing. It used to be that 50 per cent to 55 per cent of what the consumer spent on food went back to the farm gate. It is now under 50 cents on the dollar. Closer to 46 or 47 cents of every dollar goes back to the producer. That tells us the kind of services available with food. We have food that is out of season and food that is pre-packaged. It has been said many times that you do not get a potato into a modern kitchen unless it is peeled, or somehow processed. That is what consumers take for granted. Very seldom does a store not have milk in stock and on back order. A sour quart of milk is replaced without question. We are served very well by Canadian agriculture.
I wish to make a few points about the way Canadian agriculture is treated relative to the agricultural industry in some other countries around the world. Canada is a relatively small country with a population of 25 million people or thereabouts. The United States has approximately 10 times the population of Canada, as has the European Economic Community. We realize that this Government or any Government of Canada would not be able to spend the number of tax dollars supporting agriculture that either the European Economic Community or the United States is able to spend simply because Canada does not have the industrial base against which to tax in order to support agriculture. We are not suggesting that the Government give more subsidies to agriculture but we are suggesting that there are some things the Canadian Government could do. At the end of my remarks, I would like to make some specific suggestions and point out some of the things the Government could do without increasing the deficit in any substantial way.
A popular word these days is "megaproject". The oil sands has been referred to as a megaproject, as have other things. It has been said many times and is worth saying again that agriculture is an ongoing megaproject. It is a $20 billion ongoing industry. However, this means that it is easier for the Government to take the agricultural industry for granted. It is an extremely large industry, though, and involves something like 20 per cent of the labour force when including all of the service industries and manufacturing industries attached to agriculture. I would like to make sure that the Government and consumers in general understand what a large factor Canadian agriculture is in the economy.
As I said previously, we are very dependent upon exports. On average, 50 cents of every dollar that a Canadian farmer earns comes from exports. It becomes very important for the Government to do what it can to keep us competitive with our international competitors. We must remain competitive because we are not in a position to enter into any kind of a subsidy war with either the United States or the European Economic Community. It is very important for the Government to understand what happens when it starts to tax Canadian agriculture. We must have taxation systems in the country
Supply
which are as similar as possible to the taxation systems of our chief competitor, the United States.
Taking a look at the situation in the United States, something like $ 13 billion or $ 14 billion was spent by the American Government on the PIC Program. We cannot match those kinds of subsidies in this country. It therefore becomes very important that our input costs are as similar to American input costs as possible. My farm is located approximately 50 miles from the American border. A good number of people in the country live very close to the American border. If we were to go across the line and look at the input costs in the United States this spring, we would find that all of an American farmer's input costs are less expensive than they are in Canada. That includes fuel, fertilizers, chemicals, seed, machinery, repairs and everything else. A big chunk of the extra costs which we incur in Canada are the result of taxation.
Dealing with fuel, for instance, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) has told us how great the National Energy Program is because if we did not have that program and the Conservative Party had formed the Government, oil prices would have gone to world levels. The Minister has forgotten to say that a gallon of diesel fuel in the United States costs $1.20 or $1.25, yet the same gallon of diesel fuel costs 50 cents or 60 cents more in Canada. Spare us from what the Minister says is great because it is costing us more money and in fact putting us out of business.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) fail to point out that the Government places a tremendous amount of tax on farm fuels. I am suggesting that we had better be pretty careful when taxing some of these industries because to my mind, and I think a lot of people would agree with me, agriculture is a genuine creator of wealth in the country. If we do not realize this and encourage it and treat the agricultural industry as the Government treats the energy industry, this very basic, fundamental and productive industry will almost be taxed into oblivion. I can make that statement because there are a great many facts and figures to back it up, Mr. Speaker.
There are a few examples of this in southern Ontario and in fact in the Minister's riding of Windsor. In the last six weeks or so, I had a chance to talk to people who make their living in the tobacco industry. That industry is in an absolutely horrendous condition and will lose thousands of jobs this year largely because of the amount of taxation imposed by both levels of government. I am told that a package of cigarettes returns the producer something like six cents a package, yet the Government takes over $1 a package in tax. Without dealing with the morals of smoking, the point is that these producers exist and are very good at what they do. They have families and commitments and it seems to me that if we want to keep people on the land, we must look at the taxation imposed by governments.
A little over two weeks ago, I had a chance to talk to some people who work in the greenhouse industry and who are located very close to Windsor, the riding of the Minister. Those people told me that well over half their costs are

associated with energy. A big chunk of the cost of energy is tax. We should get our act together because it seems to me that we will tax these producers out of business, which, in effect, is what some of these taxes on fuels are doing. This does not mean that Canadians will not eat cucumbers, lettuce or tomatoes; it simply means that those things will be imported from the United States.
It does not make any ordinary, common, barnyard sense for a government literally to tax an industry out of business and put Canadian producers out of jobs and then, in order to satisfy consumer demand, import fruits and vegetables from the United States. I would like to refer now to the Western Grain Transportation Act, a Bill which was passed in this House last fall. We know now that the figures we were given regarding the amount of capital expenditure to be made by the railways and the number of jobs that were to be created by breaking the Crow rate were wrong. When the railways tell us that they are now going to spend something like 25 per cent less on capital expenditures than they initially said they were going to spend because their costs are down and they can accomplish the same thing by spending less money, we wonder why the Government does not come forward and decrease the costs to the producers who are going to pick up a portion of these increases. We have not seen that happen yet and it is another example of how the Government is not concerned about Canadian agriculture. The Government is prepared to see an industry taxed and, in the case of the breaking of the Crow rate, is prepared to see an industry pay more than it should, on the one hand, and pay more than it is able to, on the other. This is something which concerns a great many people.
I would like to suggest to the Government some ideas which, if implemented, would help the financial plight of Canadian farmers now at a very important time. It is now the spring planting season and people are putting their crops in the ground. These suggestions would not only help producers financially but, almost as important and perhaps even more important, they would give farmers a morale boost. Farmers know that they cannot expect governments to bail them out of all of their financial problems. I believe that most producers are very realistic in that respect. If things could be done which would not add to the deficit in any substantial measure, it would be a signal to these people that someone cares and has a little bit of understanding of their serious financial situation.
There would be encouragement and hope for the upcoming season and for the following year.
One of the things this Government could do would be to reduce the level of taxation on farm fuels. We have heard our Leader ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whether that could be done. There was an interesting exchange in the House between them and there was some concern over the deficit. But let me make a suggestion. One of the ways we could decrease the amount of money that producers need in order to put their crops in the ground this spring would be simply to stop collecting the seven cents excise tax on farm fuels which the federal Governmment collects. That could be done without increasing the deficit. This excise tax is collected and then refunded.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) is not here at the moment. He is a very beleagered Minister these days. I think that is an understatement after having seen some of the fire under which he has been in the House. Removing that excise tax would not only help the Minister of National Revenue, because he would not have to administer the program, but it would also help the producers. They would not then have to lay out the seven cents a gallon, have that money tied up with the Government for six months, or worry about filling out forms in order to get it back. Eliminating that tax would signal to the farm community that this Government has a little bit of understanding and compassion. This would not add one red cent to the deficit, and it would make good, ordinary sense.
Let me talk about what happened today concerning initial payments. Initial payments are down. The Prime Minister asked what are they. They were announced this morning. The Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) who asked the Prime Minister the question today certainly knew. It was obvious the Prime Minister did not. But initial payments are down 27 cents a bushel for hard red spring wheat. They are down 54 cents a bushel for Durum, 11 cents a bushel for six row barley, 12 cents a bushel for feed barley and they are down in the order of seven or eight cents for the two classes of oats. But the point is that initial payments are down. That is today, Friday of this week.
On Monday we saw the Farm Credit Corporation substantially increase interest rates it is going to charge farmers for new loans. I don't know how to be positive about this, but we had a very, very depressing week as far as Canadian farmers are concerned. At the beginning of the week we were told that interest rates were going up. Interest is a big cost to farmers because they are large users of capital. At the end of the week we see a Government that is not prepared to support Canadian agriculture to guarante these prices. We see grain prices reduced substantially, 27 cents a bushel, which on a percentage basis is 5 per cent or 6 per cent. That is significant. In the case of Durum, the price is down over 10 per cent. I suggest there is room on world markets for a little optimism as far as prices are concerned. My guess is that when the smoke clears,

and all the grain is sold, at the end of the coming crop year- and we are going to get a final payment-there will probably be a final payment on the prices announced today.
I see no reason why the Government should not have shown a little bit of faith in Canadian agriculture. A major researcher in western Canada resigned this week because of his disgust at the situation. I cannot remember his exact words, but he threw up his hands at where this country is going in research. This Government could take that in hand. It could show some concern, some direction and some leadership in the research field. It would not cost any additional money. There is a substantial amount of money in the federal Budget for research. One of the concerns we have is that there does not seem to be any direction. Nobody seems to know where we are going. Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words on this very important opposition day debate. One of the most important points which I feel must be brought out this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, is that immediate action has got to be taken by the Government in order to avert a crisis of some national dimension in the agricultural industry. The scenario, in effect, is building up at the present time for a substantial problem in the agricultural industry. All the signs and indications are pointing toward a very poor year in 1984 unless the Government itself really does take the problem seriously and addresses some of the questions which must be addressed.
We have a situation, Mr. Speaker, in which agricultural bankruptcies are up higher than they have been, I guess, since the Depression. The situation is building up in terms of the international grain prices which seem to be dropping. There has been some indication of just how far they may drop on the initial prices which have been made public this morning. When you start to combine these things, Mr. Speaker, and at the same time the Government seems to be turning its back on agriculture, it is plain to see that we could be in for a very, very serious problem.
Supply
I want to speak about bankruptcies, Mr. Speaker, because bankruptcy is one of the areas which is the window, in effect, through which we can see what it really happening to an industry, whether agriculture, the business sector, or any other area.
Bankruptcies in agriculture are quite substantial. The Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs reports that in 1983 some 488 Canadian farmers declared bankruptcy. That is a 19 per cent increase over the 1982 level. Bankruptcies on the Prairies jumped by 97 per cent over 1982, some 154 in total. That is startling and it certainly shows the problem we are experiencing in agriculture. We are talking only about the hard bankruptcy; one can only guess at the number of people who have gotten out of agriculture before they went bankrupt. Therefore the problem is very serious.
The Province of Manitoba, where I come from, is the hardest hit with 62 bankruptcies, up 106 per cent over 1982. This was followed by Alberta with 47 bankruptcies, a 96 per cent increase. Saskatchewan had 45 bankruptcies, an 87 per cent increase over 1982. Everything points to bankruptcies continuing at a high level this year, particularly on the Prairies. Then we have international reports which indicate an excess of grain supply, soft market prices, and the Americans will be doing a number of things to sell grain really at any cost.
In 1979, Mr. Speaker, there was one farm bankruptcy in Manitoba and a total of 125 in all of Canada. In 1980 it jumped to 14 in Manitoba, 14 in 1981 and it jumped to 30 in 1982. Then in 1983 it jumped from 30 to 62, and a total of 488 in Canada.
These figures are an indication of just how serious the situation in agriculture is. It has not really been addressed by this Government over the last number of years. Lip service has been paid by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), but nothing concrete has been done. Legislation to help the Canadian farmer in the west, in Manitoba, has not been forthcoming. The only thing we have had to deal with in a meaningful way over the last number of years is, of course, the Bill to do away with the Crowsnest Pass freight rate, which this Party fought long and hard. We were concerned about the increased costs to the western farmer, primarily the grain farmer. Of course, that is coming true and with prices dropping, bankruptcies are up, which will mean one more input cost the western farmer will have to hear for transportation to market.
Young farmers are especially hard hit. They always are because they are not established and do not have the cash reserves. In my own riding of Lisgar in southern Manitoba many young farmers got out of university, in most cases, went back to the farm, farming it on their own and are struggling, literally just hanging on, because of the poor economic situation. Many farms with large capitalizations have incomes of $8,000, $10,000, $12,000, literally below the poverty line. Such a farmer works 12 months a year below the poverty line.

First of all, there are several agricultural research laboratories throughout Canada; it is a field where the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is constantly trying to allocate additional funds to provide Canadian farmers with improved production techniques and help them increase their returns, which is not easy in these difficult times. Through his efforts and his work my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture looks quite satisfactorily, after this sector.

Prime minister was saying this morning during the Oral Question Period, we have set each year and for many years new wheat selling records, thanks to our farm producers and the Canadian Wheat Board.

There is another area, or another tool which the Government has used quite generously to help farmers make it through the difficult period we have had recently and which is beginning to fade away. As I was saying earlier in my comments, I want to take this opportunity to mention the role played by the Farm Credit Corporation and take stock of its operations.
Of course, we all agree that the agricultural industry has many problems, but I do not believe that the situation is as dark as some people would suggest. The Canadian Government provides considerable assistance to the Canadian farmers who are suffering from the backlash of the economic situation. In addition, this governmental intervention is not temporary; it does not involve ad hoc programs, but rather permanent measures, considering that the Farm Credit Corporation and its predecessor, the Farm Credit Board, have been in operation for 55 years providing Canadian farmers with financial support, management assistance and investment counselling.
To give an idea of the amounts invested in agriculture by the Farm Credit Corporation, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the Hon. Members that the corporation now has something like 80,000 loans outstanding and this represents a total investment of $4.7 billion in the Canadian agricultural industry. As the Hon. Members can see, this is an important contribution to the economic welfare of Canadian farmers.
During the fiscal year which ended thirteen days ago, on March 31, 1984, the Farm Credit Corporation has approved
some 7,536 loans under its regular credit program and its special farm financial assistance program for a total amount of $758 million. This means an increase of $141 million over the 1982-83 fiscal year. Besides, the Government has recently approved a budget which will bring up to about $825 million the amounts available to the Farm Credit Corporation for loans to Canadian farmers in 1984-85. This is definitely an increase compared with a volume of loans amounting to $7 58 million in 1983-84. The Corporation has a budget of $825 million for the year 1984-85.
Mr. Speaker, the role of the Farm Credit Corporation is helping young and new farmers, who do not have the equity required to borrow from commercial institutions. The corporation therefore has an essential role to play. As everyone knows, Mr. Speaker, new farmers and the owners of small farms who want to expand their operation are much more vulnerable because they lack personal assets, but they probably are the ones who need larger sums to develop and maintain a profitable operation and they must be able to borrow this money at favourable terms, something which the commercial sector cannot provide.
The loans with floating or frequently adjusted interest rates offered by the commercial institutions do not take into account the special features of the agricultural industry. It is very difficult for a young farmer or the owner of a small farm with little personal assets to borrow from commercial institutions at a floating rate over a period of 10, 20 or 30 years because the risks and the projections can vary too much.
The only way to help these beginners is to offer them reasonable interest rates and favourable terms, which financial institutions do not normally do. This is exactly what the Farm Credit Corporation is now doing. For instance, the corporation is offering farm enterprises loans of a maximum of $360,000 to $600,000 depending on whether the enterprise includes one or more eligible partner. The loan ceilings of the Farm Credit Corporation have been pushed up twice during the last three years to meet the needs of farmers more adequately. During a recession, the most difficult problem for farmers, as well as for small businesses and many individuals, is related to their special financing needs.
To meet these special needs and financing requirements, the Government is offering farmers, through the FCC, long term credit at terms not generally available to them or to small businesses in order to promote agricultural production. Indeed, speaking of programs developed during the last three years, especially during this period of economic difficulties, one may also mention that in addition to the Farm Credit Corporation loans, over half a billion dollars were offered to farmers to help them refinance their loans under the Small Businesses Development Bonds Program and the Special Farm Assistance Program.

I therefore believe, Mr. Speaker, that the sole purpose of all this is to promote agricultural production, to help newcomers to agriculture, especially the young farmers, and to maintain in Canada the dynamic agricultural industry we now have, which is made up of men and women whose only objective is to improve their production and increase their profits. As the Minister of Agriculture has often said, we have the chance and the privilege in Canada of having the most dynamic agricultural community in the world and its level of production compares favorably with that of any other country.
The Farm Credit Corporation puts loads of energy into its consultation services program. I referred earlier to an amount of $758 million in loans in 1983-84, but in addition to those loans, as we are dealing mostly with young farmers and small farm operators, it is important for the borrower to have a sound understanding of financial management in order to succeed. This is why the Farm Credit Corporation offers its consultation services program to its borrowers. The purpose of this program is to help farmers handle the financial management of their operation so that they will sooner or later attain their personal and economic objectives.
As a general rule, FCC borrowers who need counselling are those with little equity or sizeable debts, an expanding operation, little experience, a high risk business, or financial problems. The corporation is there to help these people by offering them a management support program for two or three years. Generally, this is long enough for them to learn to manage their financial affairs efficiently.
As of March 31, 1984, less than two weeks ago, 4,800 FCC borrowers were involved in its consultation services program, which accounts for 30 per cent of all FCC borrowers. Besides administering credit, loans and financial management assistance programs, the Farm Credit Corporation works hand in hand with federal agencies and Departments, provincial Governments and private lending institutions to meet the specific needs of farmers. For many years now, it has been cooperating with the Provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Alberta as a partner in their interest grant programs. It has renewed its efforts in that field in 1982-83 by taking part as lender in the Saskatchewan farm buying program. Last year, the FCC signed an agreement whith the Province of Ontario to make funds available under an assistance program designed for newcomers to agriculture.
Since I have only two minutes left, I would like to say in conclusion that between November 1981 and March 31 1984, the Farm Credit Corporation spent $341 million in the interest rebate assistance program. With the rebate set at four percentage points and a budget of $200 million for this program, it was possible to refund $16 million in interest rebates to Canadian farmers. As we all know, the program was extended with an injection of $100 million more in the April Budget of the Minister of Finance. When the Government established
Supply
that program, the economy recovery was expected to last for the two years of the program. The fact is that the economic recovery was very slow in the agricultural sector. As suggested by the Minister of Agriculture, the Government is now considering the possibility of extending the rebate period or certain other mechanisms to help farmers who are still in financial difficulties. As the Minister of Agriculture said recently, a decision to that effect will be made very soon, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in the Minister's remarks. He talked about partisan rhetoric and the fact that he deplored that in the Opposition. He said there was a far-fetched hypothesis around that we would form the next government. If he looks at the polls, he will realize that he was engaging in partisan rhetoric. I thought I should point that out.
Let me ask a serious question. We have suggested that one of the ways of reducing costs to both farmers and fishermen, and it would affect people from coast to coast, is for the Government to stop collecting the seven cents a gallon excise tax on fuel used on the farm and by fishermen. It would not increase the deficit because the Government collects the money and sends it back. I am sure it would help the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) and cut down on the number of steps that have to be taken. It would reduce the amount of bureaucracy involved. If anything, it would reduce government expenditure and maybe help the deficit. Would the Minister support that kind of proposal?

Mr. Speaker, I am happy the Hon. Member has asked this question. I am glad the Conservative Party has now come to this conclusion. I remind the Hon. Member that this request has been in the platform of the Liberal Party for the last four years. This suggestion has been put forward by the militants of the Liberal Party. It is being studied very closely by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). When the time comes for the Government to evaluate this issue, I will give it a great deal of attention.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister was very gracious in his reply. Could he be a little more specific? Will he do more than give it consideration? If it supported by the Opposition and his Party, surely he would not find it difficult to support that proposal and do more than give it consideration when it comes up?

Mr. Speaker, I would like my hon. friend from Portage-Marquette to realize that I am not the Minister of Agriculture. I have always supported with much passion and interest the discussions in Cabinet on agricultural issues, whether it be the red meat strategy, the Canadian food strategy or what have you. Whenever the Cabinet deals with such issues, I am vitally interested. But it is

April 13, 1984
Supply
somewhat difficult for me, without any financial data which I do not have just now, because my colleague the Minister of Agriculture is the expert in this matter to reply by yes or no. I quite understand the logic of the Hon. Member; in fact our Liberal supporters have clearly indicated during the various conventions we have held over the past few years that the removal of the excise tax on the oil products which farmers and fishermen are using would greatly reduce their production costs. I follow the Hon. Member up to that point, but I lack the necessary data to be able to give my hon. friend a yes or no answer. However, his suggestion seems to me most reasonable.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I should like to put a question to the Minister. I am sorry that I missed part of his speech. Did the Minister deal with the 4 per cent subsidy, a program which has now expired for a certain group of farmers? Maybe he did. When will the Government take a decision in that connection? Is there a chance that it will be favourable to Canadian farmers?

I thank the Hon. Member for his question, Mr. Speaker. As I said at the beginning of my speech, even if the Hon. Member represents a constituency in the core of the beautiful city of Vancouver, he is as much concerned with farming issues as all other members, because we know quite well that we owe Canadian farmers not only our fine standard of living but also our very country, because it is as farmers that our forefathers opened this country up to the West Coast.
As for the 4 per cent, I dealt briefly with it in my comments. I think that the Hon. Member is referring to the interest rebate which has been set at 4 per cent with $200 million earmarked for that program.
I said earlier that when the Government set up that program over two years ago, it expected that the recession would be over two years later. Unfortunately, as we all know, the economic recovery in the agricultural sector has been very slow. The Government is now considering a proposal from the Minister of Agriculture aimed at extending the 4 per cent interest rebate program. And my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture stated last week that he expects the Government to be in a position to make a decision soon.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join in today's debate on the Opposition motion concerning the great many problems facing agriculture today. Two days ago we in the House debated a very specific aspect of agriculture. At that time we discussed some of the financing difficulties and some very short-term solutions that might provide farmers with the means to stay in business for another year. This was important in order to see producers right across the country through the new crop year. Today's motion allows
us to expand our comments further afield and look at the broader role played by agriculture in Canada's economy. Since that is the foundation of today's motion, I would like to spend some time pointing out the role agriculture has played in the expansion of the country.
In North America, the attitude has been taken that agriculture should be used as a means of developing and expanding new lands. That was the case in Quebec, the Maritimes, Central Canada and the Prairies. Agriculture followed the fur trade and the timber trade. As timber disappeared, farms were augmented. As our economy changed from one which was dependent on exports of furs, forestry products and fish, farm products and particularly wheat were added to the economy.
The development of the agricultural base in Canada has almost been completed. Only a few million acres of land are left that could be developed for agricultural purposes and are being used for forestry or wildlife grazing lands. The development aspect of the agricultural industry is almost complete. After the development of the arable land, we moved into a second stage. Throughout most of this century we attempted to utilize technology and mechanization to reduce the number of people required to produce the same amounts or increasing amounts of food. I believe we have come a long way in that revolution and have now come to the next set of crossroads. There are now a number of decisions to make about the kind of agriculture we want in the country.
I began by saying that Canada had followed what has been a North American pattern. I simply remind you of that, Mr. Speaker, because I am going to turn for a moment to the European pattern. Europeans have been producing food on a commercial basis for much longer than we have. Their expansion process ended several hundred years ago. The mechanization program in Europe is complete and Europeans have found that taking human resources away from the agricultural industry could create limits beyond which they do not wish to go.
In Canada we are at the point now where about 4 per cent of the population lives on farms. Since the last war Europeans have been looking at policies which would keep more people on the farms. That is a reversal of the North American policies that have been followed since the war. Most of our policies have had the result, if not the intent, of reducing the number of people on farms. That reduction continues in times like these when net incomes to farmers are extremely low.
If the agricultural industry were to use an accounting system similar to that which is used in most other businesses, we would see that farmers have very little net income right now. I have pointed out many times in the House that the net agricultural income in Canada amounts to about $3.5 billion. That amount has been about the same for the last 10 years. Agriculture Canada tells us that the investment in agricultural production in the country amounts to something over $120 billion. The return on investment alone is in the neighbourhood of 3 per cent or slightly below. However, because of the way the agriculture statistics are published, that return on investment, while it would account for $3.6 billion, does nothing to supply income for the families working in agriculture. They
April 13, 1984

have a choice of paying themselves wages or paying themselves a poor return on their investment amounting to 3 per cent or 3.5 per cent. That is the reality of the situation.
Previous Canadian governments have chosen to adopt certain farm policies that would adjust to the reality that only a certain amount of net income exists. In order to increase farm incomes, the number of farmers has been reduced. Those are the policy options which have been pursued. Since the war Europeans have decided for their own reasons to pursue a policy of more self-sufficiency. I suppose that is something that we on this continent will not understand until we have lived through the horrors of a couple of world wars and until we have been starved a few times. Until that happens, we will probably find it difficult to opt for a policy of self-sufficiency. But the Europeans, having had some experience in that regard, have decided that each of the states within the European Economic Community will attempt to become as self-sufficient as possible.
The EEC have adopted policies which have the effect in our eyes of subsidizing farm production. Until recently the subsidization program went fairly well. On any food products imported into the European Economic Community, the importer paid a very high tariff. The funds raised from those tariffs were used to subsidize the production of agricultural products within the EEC. The European Economic Community has now got to the point where it is self-sufficient in virtually all major agricultural products. There is a slight surplus in some which has created a problem for the EEC. Having become self-sufficient, the EEC no longer has the income from import tariffs to subsidize its internal production. As a result, exports from the EEC combined with the surplus grains in the United States have depressed prices for grain and subsequently for all agricultural production which uses grain.
Canada has this problem and we are facing this difficulty. We have to decide some time, and debates like this are good times to raise the question, which way we should go and whether or not we should opt for more self-sufficiency in Canadian agriculture.
There are some products we clearly cannot produce, bananas being one example. One can think of a number of tropical fruits which are in demand in Canada and which we can never produce here. Anything that can be produced in a temperate zone can be produced here. There are situations where greenhouse production can operate all year round by utilizing some of the waste heat from our power stations. Even in the extreme weather on the Prairies tomatoes, cucumbers and lettuce are grown in greenhouse operations using what was before essentially waste heat. Warm air that is expelled from the manufacture of steam to drive power turbines runs through greenhouses, which aids in the production of vegetables. This operation is limited to the area around power stations and it is economical even though our border is open to the importation of fresh vegetables during the winter.
Supply
I think we must look at ways of augmenting the technology we have. Research has been mentioned a couple of times. Now we are at the stage of having to opt for a new type of agriculture. We should be watching where we put some of our research dollars.
We have developed a very high energy-use agriculture, one of the highest energy requirements per Btu of food output in the world. If you compare Canada's energy input-output ratios to that of some of the less developed countries, you would be appalled, Mr. Speaker. Our use of energy in comparison to what we get back from the food produced is only about a quarter to an eighth of the kind of input-output ratios you see in some of the so-called underdeveloped countries like Thailand or China. We have some way to go if the cheap forms of energy imported, oil and gas, are no longer as available as they were in the past.
There are some refreshing breakthroughs in biotechnology. This is probably the research area from which we will reap the most benefits. It seems to me that the development of new useful fungi moulds which can be used for creating alcohol and for attacking some of the crop pests requires far more financing than has been the case. However, it has, with its limited financing, shown some remarkable results. For instance, we have developed now a fungus that attacks the grasshopper. This fungus does not have any effect on the people who distribute the fungus in the fields. The effects of this fungus are almost as good as some of the chemicals that have been used against grasshoppers, and the danger to people and wildlife is almost zero. There are some great advantages to be gained in that area.
Along with changing the direction of agriculture, one of the first steps of which we must be cognizant is that farmers themselves must be allowed to increase their influence in the marketing of their products. We have noted with those products in which we have chosen to be self-sufficient and which we have not attempted to blast into world markets, such as dairy products, that producers have restricted their production and marketed that production to the population in Canada at rates of returns that are remunerative but not overly profitable. They have established that it is possible for farmers to produce goods and set prices in ways that will not only help the consumer to be certain of a product but will keep most of the producers of the product in business.
Products like eggs and poultry are controlled by national marketing boards which have the right to establish price on the basis of the real cost of production. That is absolutely vital if agriculture and farmers are going to be able to continue operating here in Canada. Some of the products in Canada are marketed under somewhat less stringent organizations.
I move now very briefly to the Canadian Wheat Board type of operation. Wheat is still our major export and is still subject to the price established on the so-called world market. It is established somewhere out there and we simply sell it at a price to meet the competititon.
There are some things we could be doing to provide a floor price. We did experiment briefly with the two-price wheat

April 13, 1984
Supply
system which was originally conceived by farmers to be a system which would allow them to charge a price in Canada equivalent to their actual costs and to market the balance of their production in world markets at whatever price they could get for it. Subsequently, once the proposal hit the Government and Parliament Hill, it got turned on its head. However, that is what happens sometimes with legislation once it gets here. It eventually turned out to be a way of providing Canadians with grain at a price even lower than the world price. I think the understanding of the two-price wheat system was not as well entrenched in the head of the former Minister of Agriculture, Otto Lang, as it had been in the heads of western farmers who proposed the system in the first place.
The only major area in wheat marketing where the Government has a stabilizing effect at the moment is in the establishment of initial prices. The board takes its proposals for next year's initial price, the first price the farmer receives when he delivers his grain to the elevator, and the Government underwrites that price. If the markets collapse, the Government of Canada will stand behind the price it sets and makes certain that the farmers get at least that amount of money. The tendency has been, though, for the Government to be extremely conservative on the establishment of the price. Almost always the final price is higher than the initial price and the Government of Canada does not carry any loss because the world price is higher than the Government's established price.
Today we heard that the initial prices have been established and that there is quite a marked reduction in the commitment of the Government to hold the line on grain prices, with the result of reduced prices in the order of something like 26 cents, 27 cents on red spring wheat, 54 cents on Durum, and I believe 11 cents or 12 cents on barley. Those are reductions from last year. That does not bode well for Canadian farmers who are already watching their net incomes deteriorate. They just received the message recently from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), through the Farm Credit Corporation, that the interest rates which will be available to farmers for longer term loans will be increased by one or two percentage points. The prospects for agriculture, therefore, going into this spring, are not particularly good.
I spent a little time outlining some of the directions I feel we should be looking to, but farmers going into this crop year need an injection of cash. They need the fulfilment of the promise made by the Government to change the western grain stabilization formula so it will trigger a pay-out. They would have appreciated recognition by the Government that grain prices were already low enough and that a further erosion of the price by way of reduced initial credit payments should have been avoided. They would appreciate it if that decision could be reversed.
As a result of our conventions which are held every other year, we have presented to Canadians a program for agriculture which we believe would eventually get the farmers of Canada back into a more viable position. We believe that for
the longer term we must have better marketing institutions to extract the maximum from the market. When that fails there must be, as a back-up, stabilization programs to act as insurance. For the short term, right now when farmers are faced with a critical situation, there must be an injection of credit and cash combined in order that our farmers can survive and we can get agriculture into a position where it can become again a part of the growing economy in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the two Opposition Parties for choosing agriculture as the topic for debate on two separate days this week. This shows the tremendous respect and esteem-I hope not collusion-which is felt for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) as he launches his campaign to become leader of the Liberal Party of Canada and Prime Minister of this great nation. It has certainly focused public attention on the agricultural industry and its great leader.
The Minister of Agriculture not only commands great respect in Canada, but is a man of world renown as President of the World Food Council. This man, who had his beginnings as a humble peasant from Essex County, a trait which has always stuck with him, can now run for the highest office in the land, and on his behalf I would like to thank Opposition members for their assistance in launching his campaign. I am sure that farmers across Canada join with me in wishing his every success.
It is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, that both Opposition Parties have chosen agriculture as the theme for debate this week. It emphasizes what we on this side of the House have known all along, that agriculture is one of the most basic and important sectors of the national economy. The Government is fully aware of the importance of agriculture and of the role which farmers play in the Canadian economy. There is a long list of progressive measures taken over the past few years to make sure that Canada's farming community remains strong and that the industry continues to flourish. In particular, I would draw to your attention the major items in the December, 1983 Speech from the Throne and the February, 1984 Budget. Both contained extremely positive elements for Canadian farmers.
Let us consider first several new agricultural initiatives which were announced in the Throne Speech. These are initiatives which will help strengthen the agri-food industry in both the short term and the long term. For one, there will be a commission of inquiry into the potato marketing agency in eastern Canada. The potato industry has been suffering for a long time. The Government of Canada has paid out millions dollars in recent years to help stabilize eastern potato producers' incomes, but the source of their problem appears to lie in the marketing system or, I should say, lack of one. This inquiry will get to the root of the problem.
April 13, 1984

Just two days ago I spoke in this House and referred to the fact-a fact which was referred to also by the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger)-that farmers have for too long been price takers. I suggested that they should perhaps take advantage of some of the legislation available to them, both at the provincial and federal levels, so that they can establish their price at the farm gate, a price which will reflect their cost of production plus a reasonable return on investment and labour.
I would like to read a short letter I received from one of my constituents. It is dated March 22, and I quote:
Dear Mr. Ferguson:
After being a pork producer for 10 years I have seen the effect of the ups and downs of the market, and the future does not look good. The American farmer is starting to complain about us dumping cheap pork on their market and what will happen if the hog numbers increase 40 or 50 per cent in the next three or four years.
Over the past four to six weeks I have been talking to a lot of pork producers and my feeling is that a strong majority favour a form of supply management voted through by the producers.
It seems to me that a two-price system would be what the industry needs; it is not perfect but let's work on it and make it work and then we can do away with subsidies because they do more harm than good. Subsidies are like wetting in your pants on a very cold day to get warmed up. Yours truly.
I believe this is an accurate reflection, Mr. Speaker, of some of the problems facing younger producers. I mentioned last Wednesday the fact that there really is not a countervailing force in the marketplace to ensure that the producers of Canada obtain a fair return for their products. There must be a countervailing force, whether it is in a democracy or in the marketplace. I believe we must look at this in the proper context.
I would like to refer to a few items which are available to the farmers of Canada in the way of tax provisions. First we have cash basis accounting. All farmers are permitted to use the cash basis method of accounting instead of the accrual method. This results in a considerable deferral of their tax liabilities. There is a provision for flexibility in inventory accounting. There is a provision for farm loss carry-forward which was brought in in the April, 1983 Budget. There is the five-year block averaging provision and there are the tax-free intergenerational transfers of farms.
We have a provision for clearing and improving land available as a deductible current expense. This is again a benefit to the farmers. There is a provision for farm buildings depreciation which quality for the higher rate of capital cost allowance. There is a provision for ten-year reserves. Farmers selling their farms to their children and receiving the sale price in instalments are able to establish a ten-year reserve.
There is the arbitrary expense allowance which allows fulltime farmers to deduct up to 25 per cent of all farm home expenses, including a capital cost allowance of 25 per cent on the capital cost of the farm home.
There is relief from quarterly tax payments for farmers and deferral of income on grain sales. This is available to the farmer who delivers certain types of grain prescribed under the Canada Grain Act to a licensed public elevator or a process elevator and receive a deferred cash purchase ticket. A special provision in the Act provides that the amount of the ticket can
Supply
be deferred until the following year. This is not available to us in eastern Canada but it is available to the farmers of western Canada.
We also have a deferral of income where there has been a statutory destruction of livestock. We have income splitting by paying a salary to spouse and children, the small business deduction, and then of course the investment tax credit. These are only some of the provisions available to the farm sector. Other important measures in the Budget make it easier to transfer a farm from one generation to the other. The family farm is of course the foundation of Canadian agriculture and the Government wants to keep it that way.
I am sorry I do not have a great deal of time because I have a plane to catch, Mr. Speaker, but I want to point out that Agriculture Canada is spending up to $237 million on research, up $35 million from the previous year. Our research program represents well over half the agri-food research done in Canada. I should mention that a capital improvement program for the research branch over the coming ten years amounts to more than $400 million.
Some reference should also be made to the role in international development and food aid through the support of the agricultural industry. The food that Canada provides to less developed countries through the world food program and other agencies, as well as that of our bilateral aid program, is purchased from Canadian farmers at regular prices. But the benefits go further than that. Canadian agricultural commodities given as food aid often serve to keep the door open for future export sales. Canada becomes known as a source of high quality food products. The goal of developmental aid is not to continue to feed countries which cannot feed themselves, but to help establish strong economies with commercial agricultural industries. Thus a country which is a recipient of our aid today will be our trading partner tomorrow. Exports already account for nearly half of net farm income to Canadian producers. As the world develops and our farmers become more efficient, that level will increase.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to emphasize that this Government is not ignoring the plight of Canadian farmers. We are vitally concerned about their economic health and future. Our plans and actions to date this year speak loud and clear. This Government is working on behalf of Canadian farmers, and I hope we can count on the support of all Members in this House in our efforts to improve the lot of this country's food producers.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, obviously has some influence in Cabinet. I asked the Minister about the seven cent a gallon excise tax, which is collected by the Government and then refunded. If it was not collected, it

would not add to the deficit, and it would also help farmers and fishermen this spring and on an ongoing basis because they would not have to lay out that money. I wonder if the Hon. Member is prepared to support that kind of a proposal in Cabinet?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am well aware of how the system works. You make application for a tax refund. It is the same with the Ontario provincial Government on its sales tax; you have to apply to get it back. The Minister indicated they are studying this and I would want to wait for a Cabinet decision on this issue before making further comment.

Mr. Speaker, that is a very interesting comment. He gets up and speaks on behalf of farmers, yet he is not willing to do something which makes eminently good sense to almost anyone in this country, including his constituents. Given something which is not going to add to the deficit but will benefit his constituents and assist the Government in the sense that there will be less bureaucracy and therefore less Government expenditure, surely he does not have to wait for a Cabinet decision? Surely he would be willing to push that himself in order that the Cabinet makes that kind of a decision. Is he prepared to support that kind of a proposal which would do all the things I have said on behalf of his constituents.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I indicated, the Minister replied to this. But I can tell the Hon. Member that I have been talking about this for some years and we have also been after the Ontario Tory Government to take a like position.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has quite a lot of experience on the Standing Committee on Agriculture and is now Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance. Will he bring us up to date on the agri-bond situation? Some days ago this House sent a motion to committee to investigate the whole question of agri-bonds. I understand the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs has more or less decided to accept the responsibility but has not yet struck a committee or laid out a format. Can he bring us up to date and tell us how soon we will have an active committee on agri-bonds?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this issue was referred to the committee on February 7, I believe. The Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher), moved it be sent to the committee at that time. It was discussed in committee I believe a week ago yesterday. At that time there was no background documentation available. It appears that there are several different concepts, so the committee researcher has been asked to prepare a background paper to be available to the committee when we come back immediately after the Easter break.

Mr. Speaker, could the Hon. Member tell us if he is prepared to push for the acceptance of the concept of an agri-bond which would see the agricultural sector used as a means of recycling money from the land seller to the land
buyer? Does he accept that in principle as a useful method of refinancing agriculture from one generation to the next?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it would be completely presumptuous of me to speculate on what the committee may recommend.
Go ahead. What do you think?

Mr. Speaker, just to follow up on what I think was an extremely good question from the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson) is the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and a farmer. The agri-bond concept has been referred to the committee, so surely it is not asking too much of him to say whether he supports the concept of long-range stable interest rates for farmers. That is essentially what the agri-bond does. Is he in fact in favour of trying to work out something which will assist farmers by having long-term interest rates stabilized and at a preferential rate so that more farmers can own their own land?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very much in favour of looking at some improved methods of farm financing. Whether or not the agri-bond concept is the one we should be using, I am not prepared to say until the committee is finished its work. However, I firmly believe, and I am sure the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette understands, that you cannot borrow yourself out of trouble. The farm financing package is only one in a series of requirements urgently needed in the farm sector to bring back an adequate cash flow to the farmers of this nation so they can repay their debts, keep their commitments and earn a living commensurate with that of the rest of society.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: If there are no further questions or comments we will continue with debate. The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin).

Mr. Speaker , before I begin my remarks on the motion of the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer), I would like to say that it is my own view, whether or not it is shared by colleagues in my own caucus or those of other Parties, that we should revert back to at least one part of the old rules. It shows you, Mr. Speaker, how clairvoyant I am. I will now move to the second point the Hon. Member makes, the red meat stabilization plan.
In the years that I have been here who was it that opposed any kind of national orderly marketing system for red meat? It was invariably Tories, Liberals and the Canadian Cattlemen's Association. Once the Canadian Cattlemen's Association accepts a plan for a red meat stabilization program you can bet that it will be hardly better than nothing. It will be meaningless. The Canadian Cattlemen's Association and the Saskatchewan livestock producers said to leave them alone because they wanted the free and open market system. They did not want any government interference or subsidies. As long as the market was average or better than average they were happy. As soon as their free and open market system went down the drain they were the first ones coming to Ottawa with their hands out. They are the ones who have traditionally fought against orderly marketing and fought against the Canadian Wheat Board and criticized it. I do not give a darn whether it is the cattlemen or the Palliser wheat growers or who it is. We support a red meat stabilization program that means something, Mr. Speaker. I am sick and tired of watching the majority of livestock producers, who produce the most livestock in the country, who are not ranchers and who do not belong to the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, having their prices set every bloody morning in Montreal and Chicago. Those prices bear no relationship whatsoever to their cost of production. They bear no relationship whatsoever to whether they are going to survive as livestock producers.
This nation does need a red meat stablilization plan that will in effect prevent the so-called free and open market-Safeway, Dominion and the rest of them-from setting the price of the labour and the investment of the livestock producer in Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Alberta or anywhere else in the country. The price should be set by national legislation and consultation with those actual producers, and should bear some relationship to their cost of production. If that means that in the end retail prices are too high, then how about a consumer subsidy for low and middle income families and the poor? Why saddle it on the primary producer? Let us turn it in reverse, Mr. Speaker. We too want a proper national red meat stabilization program. The kind that is being proposed at best might be slightly better than nothing. Everyone supports passing legislation on increased advance payments and motherhood. The way things are now, the maximum advance payments should be even higher than what is in the proposed legislation. Resist erosion of initial payments.
Last year and the year before we in the NDP, many economists and many people in farm organizations warned about what is going on in the international grain market. A month ago I read another article about what is happening with our major competitors and the amount of grain they have in storage, their excess production and the amount of subsidy they pay to their grain producers. It was the same government, aided and abetted by the Official Opposition who said that that did not matter and that they would still raise the freight

rate. The Conservatives said they would not do it tomorrow, they would do away with the statutory grain rates two years from now. Of course, they voted against Bill C-155.
