Mr. Speaker, the Tory Party hired the guy who wrote the Bill. He was kept on to finish the work by the Liberal Government. They are not going to get away with that out West.
We will see after the next election.

Of course we have to stop the erosion of initial payments. What they mean is that when the Canadian Wheat Board must cut prices in order to maintain or get new contracts, the difference between the maximum it receives from an exporter and what the grain producers should receive would be made up from the National Treasury. It is a subsidy that not only benefits the grain producer but the entire nation.
It is time to reinstate what was called the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. I remember the episode when a former Minister of Transport succeeded in eliminating that. Where were the Tories at that time? Our Party was able to have farmers take the Government to court and they had $100 million returned to them. The Temporary Wheat Reserves Act simply meant that the nation as a whole paid the storage charges for any grain in excess of a certain amount in storage. It saved our grain producers $75 million to $100 million a year. However, the Government did away with it, and it was aided and abetted by the Official Opposition. That Act should be reinstated.
The Hon. Member's motion also raises the issue of the Western Grain Stabilization Act. Our Party succeeded in stopping the Government in its first attempt to introduce it. On the second occasion the Official Opposition sat in both the Transport Committee and Agriculture Committee and meekly accepted it even though-
Where were you yesterday?
I was there.
Where were you last week? Did you hear our leader?
The Leader of the Opposition discovered the Western Grain Stabilization Act just about a week ago.
Why did you defeat it?

The Western Grain Stabilization Act was designed to take grain producers' money. There is more than
$1 billion in the fund and the Government still has not put up its share. No interest has been collected on this money. When this Act does come into effect, the highest payment is made to the producer who delivers the most grain. The smaller payment will go to the producer who must travel up to 40 miles to the elevator, who is only on his second quota, whose road is closed because of snow or spring thaw, and who is unable to deliver as much grain.
If the unemployment insurance plan was run on the same basis, when unemployment reached a certain level and triggered a payment from the fund, the person who was working full time would get the biggest payment. Surely that is backwards. If the national medicare program was run on the same basis, it would mean that when the number of patients that went to doctors and hospitals exceeded a certain amount and triggered a payment, the person who was never sick a day would get the biggest payment.
That is why the Western Grain Stabilization Act needs to be amended to trigger a payment, and the highest payments should go to those who need it the most. That is what we argued for in the first and second Grain Stabilization Bills that were brought in the House, beginning in 1970.
The motion also calls for a reduction in high interest rates. The former Minister of Finance of the Official Opposition supported two Liberal Ministers of Finance in two ways. First, he supported them in not firing Gerald Bouey and, second, he said he would do the same thing if he were still the Minister of Finance. He would also artificially prop up the Canadian dollar and raise interest rates to keep the Canadian dollar as high as possible. This costs grain produceres, fishermen, the forest industry and all our exporters more at home and raises the costs of our exports. We lose both ways. I am not concerned about what the Canadian dollar is worth compared to the American dollar, the Fiji dollar or the "Pango-Pango" dollar. I am more concerned about what it is worth to Canadians and what it is doing for us here in Canada.
I believe we should take some of the steps that Louis St. Laurent and John Diefenbaker took in pegging the Canadian dollar, pegging interest rates and implementing foreign exchange control, as was done shortly after the Korean War and again in 1958 or 1959, because it assisted all of our primary producers in forestry, the fishery, the grain industry and in livestock. It helped all of our exports. It made imports more expensive so that Canadians bought more goods made in Canada. Why do we not try that again? This program worked when it was applied in wartime.
Grain producers cannot be expected to survive when they are faced with higher freight rates, higher interest rates and higher costs on all their farm inputs while their prices are reduced even further. The nation as a whole must share in the cost of maintaining a viable agricultural industry, whether it is grain on the Prairie or livestock in Ontario, on the Prairies, in Quebec or other parts of Canada.

What about apples?

April 13, 1984

Apples, fruits and vegetables; the Government should be investing in the using of excessive heat capacity in a massive greenhouse operation so that we can grow fruits and vegetables during the winter instead of paying $2 or $3 for cauliflower grown in California or Florida. It can be done. Unless primary producers can be assured a decent price and a decent living from their products, they will not survive. How many more years must we go through patchwork and ad hoc measures? When will the Government learn?
The European Economic Community, Argentina and Australia make sure that their producers get a fair price. The Americans will not sit idly by with their surpluses. They will cut their prices. The Government is asking Canadian primary producers to compete against the Treasury of the United States. Surely that is not fair, because the wealth of the entire nation is needed to accomplish that.
I mentioned the matter of grain in storage. We should return to the system where the nation as a whole shares the storage costs of grain. Even during tough times, having grain in store for export sales is like having money in the bank. But that money is for the entire country because the grain producer who has had to pay the cost of growing it cannot afford to keep it. However, this grain in storage is an asset for the entire country and we should share in the cost of its storage, whether it is on the farm, at an inland elevator terminal or export terminal. Surely that is a fair proposition and one that makes good sense. It is done by other countries.
Our agricultural community continues to diminish. What will those thousands of farmers who lose their farms every year do? Money that is spent in the agricultural industry is not an expense but an investment in this country which benefits the entire nation. While the entire country shares in the costs, it also shares in the return on that investment. These costs which may consist of guaranteed initial prices with any difference made up by the national Government, a real grain stabilization income plan or these other programs included in the Hon. Member's motion, should be shared by the entire nation.
I hope that the Government, in its last, gasping days, will implement programs such as those. It will see how well they will be received by the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and privilege to speak on this agricultural motion this afternoon. This is an important subject, particularly in my riding of Ontario. Many people think that I come from an urban riding; many of my voters as well as some of the gentlemen at the table. I want to explain that my riding on a geographical basis
April 13, 1984

is 90 per cent agricultural and less than 10 per cent urban. I do have a constituency that is most concerned.
I want to mention another point. 1 have sat in this House for almost five years. My duty day has been Friday. Today is a low point in attendance. There are more people in the gallery than on the floor of the House of Commons. Something should be stated to shame the Liberals who are responsible for having 20 Members here at all times. It is a disgrace.
One of the basic problems facing our entire economy, not only agriculture, is that we have been totally misled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). On April 11 in New York City he stated we do not consume 90 per cent of private savings for fiscal expenditures. My researcher worked out the figures. He stated we only spend 25 per cent. The figure for 1982 was 83.7 per cent. Today it is over 90 per cent. It is the fiscal approach and fiscal misleading which has caused the trouble.
There are a number of small farmers in my riding. Most legislation has been of little or no benefit to them. For example, there was the creation of Canagrex. I would like someone opposite to tell me what Canagrex has accomplished. It has a staff and a budget and it spends money. It was intended to create revenue for Canada, but it has done nothing. It has tried to interfere with the private sector and has failed.
Members opposite are always knocking the private sector. The private sector is the only thing that will save this country, but the Government does nothing to assist it. I will give an example. I have spoken many times in this House and have asked many questions, but to date I have not received an answer about Canadair and de Havilland which have collectively cost this economy $6 billion. If a little piece of that $6 billion had been directed with equity and fairness to the farmers of Ontario, there would not be the problems we have read about in the papers in the last few years.
Part of the farmers' problems has come about because of Section 31 of the Income Tax Act. Section 31 was designed for hobby farmers. The Department of National Revenue has applied that to legitimate farmers with small farms, those trying to hold the farm together. The Department applied that Section to those who had to leave the land during the off season, or winter season. Together with help from their spouses and children, they did the chores in the morning and at night. This Section was imposed on these farmers who could not afford the expensive equipment when the price of their produce remained at a fixed level. Inflation affected the price of equipment. Applying Section 31 has, therefore, been damaging, yet the Government has collected very little compared to the tremendous waste in the aerospace industry. That industry could have been a success with proper management, but it failed. There is proper management in the agriculture industry. I do not know of any group of people with a better basic understanding of economics than farmers. I probably learned more from my neighbours than anybody I have heard in this
Supply
House or from any papers I have read. They have a basic belief that unless you have, you do not spend. They believe you must save. If you cannot afford something, you find a way to pay for it.
I wish to give an example of the inequity of Section 31. If these people had incorporated in such a way that they could be paid by a corporation, that Section would have been applied to the farm corporation and they would not have been hurt. However, the Department of Revenue would have caught up with that. Many people use methods under the tax system to avoid tax which are not permitted to the farmers. I object to that.
I dwell on this point because the family unit in Canada is important. We have become dependent on the state. It is time that we became dependent on ourselves and on our own efforts. Farm people are dependent on their own efforts. They have been the creation of our society and the success of our export program. We have let them down. The way the Government invoked the Crowsnest Pass rate, if it had not been for this Party and our amendments, it could have been total destruction of western farmers. Also, it directly affects farmers in eastern Canada.
We have heard vague talk about the red beef stabilization program. Ontario could not wait for the federal Government so it brought in its own program. It could wait no longer. There was such ill treatment that they had to move on their own. If the provinces can bring in such a program, why not the federal Government? It is because the federal Government has not co-operated with the provinces. It will not sit down and work out joint programs. No wonder this country is so split apart. It is because there have been no federal-provincial negotiations. That is one of the first things our government will do after an election is held. We have friends from coast to coast. We are friendly with governments from coast to coast. We have a common purpose, to help Canada. All the Liberals plan for is retaining power, and the Canadian citizens be dammed. I hope the election comes soon.
There are two remarkable items in Ontario that have been accomplished by the Ontario Department of Agriculture, namely, egg advertising and pork advertising. It has assisted to a great extent. Pork producers in my riding could not have survived if they had not been brought together by the provincial minister to work out a program to assist in selling their product across the border. Pork has been somewhat unstable in price in the past. Because of the programs of the Ontario Government, it has stabilized very definitely.
There is another point which, as a previous speaker mentioned, affects Ontario and British Columbia. A ban was placed on fruit on which certain chemicals had been applied. That ban was domestic. It did not apply to vegetables brought into this country from other lands. I do not understand how we can treat our fruit farmers in a negative way, compared to those in other lands. This is an inequity in the system which has been created by the federal Government. It shows that the Government has no heart, it has no feeling for the people. To put something like that in place is wrong. What is good for the

goose is good for the gander. If it is good for people in the southern United States, then it must be good for Canadians. I agree that there must be some restriction on certain chemicals which appear to have toxic residue, but we should not impose that restriction only on ourselves.
An issue which has been close to my heart for many years is the possibility of irrigation in Ontario. The Province of Ontario has been blessed by having available to it approximately 50 per cent of the world's supply of water. We must address the issue of producing more food here in Canada and this can be tied into the remarks made earlier about the programs for greenhouses. A great deal of the food produced in Canada is not of as high a quality as the food brought from the United States because the food has not had the chance to grow. There are more facilities in the United States for irrigation than in Canada.
We must try to improve quality and I know that Canadian farmers are capable of doing so. However, they need assistance in order to implement irrigation. Irrigation is very expensive but it could guarantee supply and quality. This is a subject which must be dealt with through federal-provincial discussions. In the future, there may be another dust bowl like the one of the 1930s. It will be then that Ontario could become so important to the production of grain. I feel that this is another very important issue which should be approached.
I recently read an article about interest rates and farmers. As I understand it, the Farm Credit Corporation was created to help farmers get reasonable loans. Under the present program, any farmer who would borrow money on a 20-year term with a 15 per cent interest rate would not make a red cent. He | should put his money in the bank so he could get a 15 per cent return on his money. These extended loans are ridiculous because they are being given to farmers at a cost which they cannot afford. If we are going to do something, we should do it in a reasonable way.
The Province of Ontario has a much smaller revenue base than the federal Government, but the provincial Government of Ontario has a program that assists beginning farmers. This program gives a rebate on Farm Credit loans with interest rates that exceed 8 per cent. At least the provincial Government is being realistic. It knows that a farmer cannot afford to pay an interest rate of more than 8 per cent. There has been much instability of interest rates, and that is why a return to Section 31 of the Income Tax Act is inequitable. I know that the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) is fully aware that people are having to borrow money to make the interest payments on money borrowed for equipment purchases.
Many people have said that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is marvellous, and how great it is that he has entered the leadership campaign. They hope he wins the leadership campaign, and then perhaps agriculture will benefit because he will be running the Liberal Party and will not have as much time to do anymore damage to the agricultural
community in Canada. If he was serious, Mr. Speaker, he would have fought for reasonable interest rates. I realize that dealing with the Minister of Finance is like beating one's head against a brick wall but I am sure that after four years, the Minister of Agriculture could have gotten the message across.

We want positive approaches; we need positive approaches to get the country moving and help the agriculture community. The people in my riding are sick and tired of this Government that really does not understand agriculture and really does not have any representation from the agricultural community West of the Manitoba border. I understand the feelings of those people.

However, I would like to say that every member on the government side should read that Budget which was brought down in March of this year.
What is the deficit?

The financial position is in excellent shape, and the deficit is a lot lower than the National deficit. That Budget has provided the fuel to ignite the engine of the economy. The Budget will help small business people, and it includes a program for the agricultural community which is probably one of the finest I have seen come from a provincial Government.
The Hon. Minister of Agriculture could have implemented such a program. He has failed his country. He has failed the farming community. He has not had a strong enough voice. He has not let the consumers know about the importance of the providers of food.
I have heard many people speak about inequities for farmers, but unless one has been there one does not know what it is like. I have heard it mentioned as compensation that farming is a wonderful way of life. It is a wonderful way of life. I myself live on a farm. I like the outdoors and I like to see the country side from my windows. However, it has become almost impossible for small family units to exist on a farm. If these family units cannot exist, that increases the number of unemployed people who must be provided for either through unemployment insurance or the welfare system. I do not know many farmers who would accept help from the welfare system because they are proud Canadians. They are a credit to the country and they should not have to be put in this position.
I saw your signal, Mr. Speaker, indicating that my time is up. I appreciate having been afforded the opportunity to

express the view of the agriculture community in the riding of Ontario and I hope that someone listens to some of the points we have made today.

One of the things that interested me this week, Mr. Speaker, was the announcement by the Minister of Agriculture that he had received Cabinet approval of a tripartite stabilization program for the red meat industry. That represents an historic step forward in the Canadian livestock sector. Red meat producers have been plagued with marketing problems for years, and agreement in principle on a stabilization plan by producers, some provinces and the federal Government climaxes more than ten years of discussion, debate and negotiations. I think it was the Hon. Member who asked, "why did it take so long? Why do provinces have to move on their own?" If we are going to get into a Canadian stabilization program we have to deal with different provinces with different priorities and different ideas about how a stabilization plan can be made to work on behalf of the producers.
Agriculture is a shared jurisdiction by federal and provincial governments in Canada, and the achievement of a general agreement to proceed with a red meat stabilization plan demonstrates the ability of the federal Government and the provinces to co-operate for the benefit of farmers in this country. There has been co-operation through a whole series of fields between the federal Government and either individual provinces on a bilateral basis where that might be necessary, or on a multilateral basis where we have to bring all of the provinces in to a particular area because of the particular problems being faced by Canadians-in this case by the Canadian farmer, the red meat people.
Livestock producers have been particularly hard hit by the world wide recession and inflation. Unlike their colleagues in the poultry and dairy sectors, they have not had the protection of supply management to keep prices in line with their production costs. The new stabilization program will go a long way toward evening out the ups and downs in the red meat industry and allowing producers to plan their production with greater security.
That word "security" has a tendency from time to time to be over-used, and yet it is so important. I find that responsible union leaders from time to time are as much concerned these days about job security as they are with increases or pension plans being put in place.
When operating in the marketplace, where there are so many variables that are beyond the ken and the control of the red meat producer, I think it is appropriate that a stabilization plan be put into place. Whether this is the best one for Canada or Canadian red meat producers I do not know. I am not an expert or a professional in the field, but it seems to me that common sense would dictate that something along this line has to be done. We have seen it done, as I have said, on a province-wide basis, and now it is time to move, hopefully, to the Canada-wide situation.
I think it is important to point out that this plan was worked out in full consultation with the producer organizations. The Minister mentioned on Monday that an agreement on a red meat stabilization plan represents a minor miracle of co-operation among producers, federal and provincial governments. As I indicated earlier, we have a tripartite kind of agreement which is even more difficult than dealing solely with the producer or the provincial governments.
I think a few more minor miracles may be needed before the plan is fully effective for all livestock producers in Canada. I am advised that Members opposite can help in achieving those miracles by co-operating in speedy passage of the enabling legislation necessary for the plan to go into effect. This legislation I am given to understand is expected to be introduced in the very near future, most assuredly in my view before June.
As all Hon. Members know, we have an Agricultural Stabilization Act in effect, and have had for many years. Since 1978 the federal Government has put more than $200 million into the red meat industry in stabilization payments to beef, pork, and lamb. This is just one more indication of the kinds of money we are talking about in terms of helping Canadian farmers.
The new tripartite proposal represents a major step forward in several ways. First, it involves producer participation. Farmers will have a direct stake in this plan. Second, it commits all provinces which join the plan to the same level of support. Top loading by provinces and the balkanization of the industry which it has caused has been a serious problem. That has been one of the defects, the kind of thing the Hon. Member for Ontario raised, that a particular province or provinces had to go it alone, because it did lead to balkanization, which I believe in Canada is inappropriate, certainly not in the best interests of the producer.
How do we work out a plan which is Canada-wide and which wins the acceptance of the federal and provincial Governments and the producers themselves? That is no mean feat. While I sympathize with provinces wishing to help their producers, I am sure they must all realize that a uniform set of
April 13, 1984

policies for farmers across Canada is in the long-term interest of the industry.
I feel the most important benefit of the new program will be the speed with which it will respond to price fluctuations. Under the present Act, once a stabilization payment has been announced, producers have to submit their claims and those claims must be verified before the cheques can go out. Under the new plan, producers will be preregistered and their eligibility will already be established. In all the new plans, except the one for the cow-calf operators, support prices will be calculated quarterly. This means that when payments are warranted, they can be made quickly. I believe that has been the failing, Mr. Speaker, all too often of government programs, be it federal or provincial. When a program promises you something but you have to wait for it, there is a detrimental effect or a worrying effect on the people who are entitled to that particular payment and should not have to wait for it.
I ran into that, Mr. Speaker, all too often with unemployment insurance payments where people anticipated receiving a certain amount of money within a certain period of time. I must say, to the credit of the people who work for the Unemployment Insurance Commission, they have made many splendid moves which have brought about, in the vast majority of cases, prompt payment to people who have paid a premium for insurance.
If this program had been in effect last year, my information is that cow-calf producers would have received $29.7 million; producers of backgrounder cattle, $8.3 million; feed lot operators, $12.4 million; hog producers, $92.4 million and lamb producers $3.9 million. The key features of the new program are; first, that provinces and producers may join on a voluntary basis; second, that the federal Government, participating provinces and producers will contribute equal amounts of money to a stabilization fund; third, separate plans will be offered for cow-calf producers, beef backgrounders, slaughter cattle finishers, hog producers and sheep producers; fourth, payments from the fund will be made when market prices fall below the national support level; and five, the level of support will not be high enough to become an incentive to over-production.
Support prices for beef backgrounders, slaughter cattle and hogs will be based on a guaranteed margin approach, while support prices for calves and sheep will be based on an average weighted price reflecting the impact of inflation.
I am advised, Mr. Speaker, that in this kind of legislation, in this particular instance, the agriculture stabilization board will administer the new plan with guidance from a nine-member red meat stabilization committee. Like the plan itself, that committee will represent the three parties involved, the federal Government, the provinces and the producers. There will also be a consultative committee for each commodity, thus ensuring that those involved in production of red meat products have a continued input into the operation of the plan.
We must be careful, Mr. Speaker, in putting something in place to recognize that there could be defects and there should be some plan or means whereby that particular program can be improved upon and improved upon immediately. Sunset
Supply
clauses all too often come in and wipe out the whole operation.
I believe that is inappropriate, certainly for an operation like this. We must constantly look and check, and constantly pay attention to where the problems are, whether this is done by the consultative committee or by members of the stabilization board or the advisory committee. This is a situation where people will have an opportunity to determine where the program has flaws and to bring about improvements.
I want to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that this is a voluntary program and full consultation with the producers and the provinces will be maintained throughout the next stages as the program develops. The enabling legislation, as I indicated earlier, will be introduced soon. I see this as a major step forward in support of a very important sector of the agriculture industry, and one which will be watched carefully by producers of other commodities and by other countries. I think it is fair to say, Mr. Speaker, that it is but one more example of the innovative, creative, consultative approach which this Government has taken to encourage the agriculture industry.
I learned a fair amount about farming, Mr. Speaker, when I served as the county solicitor, but I feel I learned a great deal more about politics. On one occasion I was with the Reeve of Alvinston, the late Clayton Cox. We had to go about some important county business in Alvinston. I drove from Sarnia to Alvinston, which is a fair distance, and met him at his home. From there we were going to the place where we were holding the meeting. He kept talking to people and shaking hands and I said, "Come on, Clayton, we have to get moving". He said, "Bud, this is a small town. If I lose that side of the street, I lose the election". They know what democracy is all about in the rural part of our country, Mr. Speaker.

There were some rather interesting comments made today. One comment made me prick up my ears. I heard a Government Member talking about getting payments out on time when people need them. That is a very pertinent comment to the people of Okanagan and to the industry I represent, and, I am proud to say, myself. I still have my orchard. I received a letter from the Minister on March 5. He was very pleased to tell me about a stabilization payment for the 1982 apple crop. I am not sure that all the growers in the Okanagan have received their payments yet. The 1982 crop was fully harvested and in storage by November 1 and probably most of it was stored by October 15 of that year. I was also interested in the dialogue between the Government Member and the Hon. Member for the New Democratic Party concerning deficits, whether they are good or bad, and whether they should be increased or decreased. The argument, from our standpoint, is not that we need to increase deficits in order to do some of the things which should be done in the country, but that we need a Government which is prepared to stop doing things which should not be done in the country and change its priorities for spending. I do not think we are participating in increasing the deficit, we are just going to displace about $5 billion now being misappropriated and put it to more useful purposes.
Tell us what you would do.
We will demonstrate in less than a year's time if you guys ever get the courage-
We have to get a leader first.

Well, you have quite a selection now.
The Royal Bank in advertising its Royfarm banking service for farmers in the magazine Farm and Country used a picture of a needlepoint wall hanging which very prominently states:
If you don't know where you have been and where you are, it's hard to plan where you're going.
I would like to hang one of those in the office of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). Perhaps we could have one hand made by some hard pressed farmer's wife as a constant reminder to the Minister: "If you do not know where you have been and where you are, it is hard to plan where you are going". Farmers across Canada generally have reason to doubt that the Minister knows where the farmer has been, what they have been through, and certainly we doubt that he understands where the farmer is presently at. As the motto says, it is hard, Mr. Minister, to plan where you are going under these circumstances. We would like to help him, but more particularly help the Canadian farmers.
In forming the next Government of Canada, the Progressive Conservative Party will do just that. It is appropriate indeed that we consider the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) on behalf of the Progressive Conservative Members of Parliament, the farmers' friend, I might add. The motion says:
That whereas the economic problems facing Canadian farmers today are largely the result of Government in-action and neglect, this House condemns the Government for its failure to recognize the importance of the agricultural sector and its contribution to economic growth in Canada-
The present Minister of Agriculture will be rather too preoccupied with his own leadership ambitions to put his energies and efforts to helping fulfil the ambitions of Canadian farmers. These days that ambition is simply to survive to meet their obligations, pay their bills and avoid losing their farms, homes, assets and their usefulness to society.
I was interested to see the interview by Pamela Wallin of the Minister of Agriculture on this morning's TV show. Her intuitive questioning of the Minister contained in it much of the reason behind the farmers' grave difficulties today. Her question was something like this: Why are you, the Minister of Agriculture, trying to become the leader of the Liberal Party of Canada, a Party that really has little interest in rural Canada and relates almost exclusively to urban Canada? Those are not the exact words but that is the gist of her question. I believe that demonstrates the root cause of the malaise in agriculture in Canada; a Government which really does not have that much interest in the subject. This is convincingly demonstrated by the statistics available to all which tell a very sad story of neglect by this Government.
We need look no further than the record of farm bankruptcies, Mr. Speaker, which provides an index of escalating difficulties experienced by Canadian farmers. In 1980 bankruptcies were up 77 per cent over 1979. In 1981 they were up a further 17.6 per cent. In 1982 they were up 57 per cent again. In 1983, up 19.6 per cent. In January and February, 1984, bankruptcies are up 58.3 per cent over the same period in
1983.	If we assume the number of bankruptcies in 1975 as the base, or 100, the bankruptcy index in 1984 has now reached 620. That measures the degree of anxiety, anger and terror which exists out in the real world of agriculture; out there, Mr. Speaker, where the wheat is growing, the cattle are raised, the eggs produced and, of course, the apples, peaches and cherries are cultivated, nurtured and harvested. It is in that real world that the massive instability is ending in tragedy for a great number of farmers, and there is no prospect in sight of major relief from these difficulties. There is no prospect except the anticipated federal election which will change governments, change Ministers and change an entire philosophy toward government responsibility to agriculture in Canada.
In a statement of Members of Parliament dated April 11,
1984,	the Canadian Federation of Agriculture said that surely a modest degree of assistance and assurance of reasonable stability in interest rates, plus reasonable measures of price stability, are a small price to pay to help ensure the preservation of the family farm structure of Canadian agriculture. If the family farm is to be preserved, Mr. Speaker, special farm credit measures must be taken. Today's interest rates are simply not affordable. The question might be asked: Does the Government recognize this fact?
I called the British Columbia Federation of Agriculture to ask them what their chief concerns in British Columbia were today. They gave me three subjects: Stabilization is first and foremost on the mind of B.C. farmers; Section 31 harassment by Revenue Canada is No. 2; third, the Farm Credit Corporation. They said there is a disenchantment that it has come to be the lender of last resort without adequate funding.
The B.C. Federation of Agriculture said recently that to achieve economic recovery and long term prosperity in British Columbia we must recognize and build upon our economic strengths. Agriculture is one of these strengths. The industry contributes $2.5 billion in wholesale sales to the 1982 gross

provincial product, a 4 per cent increase over 1981 and a 14 per cent increase over 1980. At a time when other resource industries were hard hit with declines in production and numbers employed, agriculture continued at pre-recession levels. Agriculture is the mainstay of rural communities, stabilizing regional economies. Approximately 65,000 people are kept working in the British Columbia agriculture and food industry. Fifty-five per cent of the food consumed in B.C. is produced in the province by less than 1 per cent of the population. That is the good news in B.C.
The bad news is that net farm income in B.C. is plummeting. The share of the consumer dollar which comes to the farmer is shrinking. The input costs of production to the farmer are skyrocketing. These are facts faced by farmers right across Canada. The dilemma is particularly acute in British Columbia where costs have outstripped ability to pay. These costs are outside the farmers' ability to control.
Take for instance the Okanagan tree fruit farmers growing cherries, apricots, peaches, apples, prunes and pears. Fruits so attractive and so mouthwateringly good must be retailing at a price which puts money in the farmers' pockets, right? Wrong. The 1983 peach crop returned 2.942 cents a pound from the market to the fruit farmers in the Okanagan. That is $58.84 a tonne for the best peaches produced anywhere in Canada, or anywhere in the world.
I first got into fruit farming on my own in 1955 in Kaleden where my father planted the first orchards in 1912. Back in the 1950s and 1960s we used to pick the peach crop and wonder whether we would get three cents a pound. Sometimes we got four cents, sometimes we got less. That was 25 years ago when orchard labour was 75 cents an hour or less as compared to $6 to $10 an hour now. The three cents a pound for peaches in 1961 meant that eight or nine pounds of peaches would buy a gallon of farm fuel. Today with the market returning three cents the orchardist must pick nearly 70 pounds to buy that same gallon of fuel. It is a tough world out there and someone must recognize that fact.
The Minister's response is to tell B.C. farmers that if their province helps them financially the federal Government will penalize them. What a farce. The federal Government is telling B.C. farmers that they are expendable and their situation is not recognized, so tough luck boys and girls.
There are so many little things the Government could be doing to encourage farmers. How about the elimination of the 9 per cent sales tax on fuels used in food production? That would not cure everything, but it would indicate a substantial interest in agriculture. How about taking note of the resolutions which came out of the sixty-second annual meeting of the Canadian Horticultural Council held here in Ottawa in March? A number of them dealt with the complexity and confusion which pertains to deductions; unemployment insurance, Canada pension, workmen's compensation, income tax and other mandatory deductions.

In a resolution the council asked for some uniformity in the formula of the hours worked and the amount earned that would trigger the deduction processes. I wish the Government would recognize the burden that this adds to the farming community. If very often increases the amount of work the farmer has to do in the evening after his daily chores on the farm have been completed.
The fact is that fruit farmers in the Okanagan have their backs to the wall. The industry that produces economic stability in that beautiful area of British Columbia may very well not survive in its present state through this decade. The large part of the competition for markets comes from Washington State where all cost inputs, fuel costs, costs of irrigation, insecticides, fertilizers and, most notably, the cost of labour, are dramatically lower. -packing-house workers and employees working for Tree Fruits in B.C. received $12.50 an hour, while across the line in Washington State, the same workers receive $4.70 to $5.25 an hour.

In those five years he should have learned that when dealing with government business it is up to our side to provide the quorum, and if it is an Official Opposition day it is up to them to provide a quorum. When they started their debate this morning, they had three people here.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis) just brought to our attention something which is entirely new to me. It is the fact that on Opposition days it is supposed to be the Opposition which has 20 people here to form a quorum, and on government days the Government is supposed to make a quorum. Quite frankly, I have never heard of that order. Perhaps he would be kind enough to give us the reference from whence he gets this.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: First, I do not consider that a point of order. It is a point of discussion. We will return to debate.

Mr. Speaker, I think it would make common sense that if they bring in a motion they should have the troops here to debate it-not three people. At 2.30 o'clock, one Tory Member was here. I have been watching their ranks all afternoon. That is the Party which was expressing its great concern about the agricultural sector.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I prepared a speech and obviously I will not be able to deliver it. I just do not understand the remarks of the Hon. Member. I think my point of order is well taken.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to advise the Hon. Member that that is not a point of order.
A point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will recognize the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) on a point of order, but I would appreciate it if he would come directly to his reason for rising.
Is it not a fact, Sir, that there are three times as many members of the Opposition presently in the Chamber as there are members of the Government?

Four times as many.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That is not a point of order.
But it is a fact.

The motion of the Hon. Member for Portage-Mar-quette (Mr. Mayer) attempts to condemn the Government for failing to recognize the importance of the agricultural sector. Among other subjects, the motion makes specific reference to several initiatives affecting the western grain industry. I would like to draw to his attention the investment of the federal Government since 1973 in the purchase and leasing of hopper cars. This represents money saved for western farmers.
I have one eye on the clock, and I will save the time of the House by not giving the details of that, other than to say that total federal spending under the Crow which will go into branch line rehabilitation and hopper car purchases will amount to $8.9 billion in the decade between 1983 and 1992. The mover of the motion laughs when I bring this to his attention. He was the one who boycotted Bill C-155 all summer and all fall. He was the one who stalled. Now he and his colleagues want passage of a Bill in an hour, after they wasted months and months of the valuable time of this House.
What a bunch of garbage.

This is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was talking about when he said to the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Mulroney), "get your act together, show a little co-operation and we can pass a lot of Bills through the House".
Let the people decide.
Yes, let the people decide.

The Government hopes that this Bill can be passed before the start of the new crop year on August 1. Under the proposed amendments, the maximum advance for individuals will double from $15,000 to $30,000. Other changes include increasing the limit for emergency advances for drying tough and damp grain from $1,000 to $3,000, and for unthreshed grain from $7,500 to $15,000.
The Opposition motion urges the Government to resist the erosion of initial payments. Just this morning the Hon. Senator Hazen Argue, Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, announced in Regina initial payments for the 1984-85 crop year. Senator Argue said that on August 1 the initial payments for spring wheat will decrease $10 per tonne, for feed oats they will increase $20 per tonne, for feed barley and designated oats they will increase $10 per tonne, and that for durum and designated barley they will drop only $5 per tonne from levels set a year ago.
Only!

The reductions in wheat payments reflect abundant supplies in relation to world markets and continuing pressure on prices, while the increases reflect more buoyant markets for feed grains.

April 13, 1984
Supply
Despite the difficult outlook for the 1984-85 crop year with respect to wheat, the Government has maintained initial payments as close to last year's levels as possible. That was the intent of part of the Hon. Member's motion. The Government's objective is to assist in maintaining farm cash flow at as high a level as possible, even if it poses a slightly higher risk of deficits in the pool accounts of the Wheat Board, which would have to be underwritten by the federal Treasury.
Even though some initial payments are slightly reduced, Senator Argue has indicated that he would be prepared, if market conditions significantly improve, to recommend that an adjustment be made in the initial payment levels either before August 1, if possible, or after the start of the new crop year.
In today's announcement, Senator Argue noted that once again this year grain exports are moving well-about 5 per cent ahead of shipments in the 1982-83 crop year. Car unloads are up about 2 per cent overall, including a 14.8 per cent increase at Thunder Bay.
That is because the Hon. Member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Mazankowski) was Minister of Transport five years ago.

However, there is no doubt the situation in world grain markets is difficult and competition is tough. In these very competitive circumstances, the Canadian Wheat Board is doing an excellent job of marketing prairie grain. The longterm agreements negotiated by the Wheat Board with its customers guarantee minimum sales of 14 million tonnes. Also it should be noted that any substantial reduction in crops in main producing areas in the current crop year could bring about a strengthening of world grain prices.
The Opposition motion also urges the Government to pass urgently-needed amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act. Hon. Members will be aware that the Government made a commitment in the Speech from the Throne to introduce amendments to this legislation to make it more responsive to the needs of western farmers.
When?

That need was recognized by this side of the House long before the Leader of the Opposition discovered the other week that western farmers have a problem. I am sure Hon. Members of all Parties will support these amendments when they are brought before the House in the near future.
When?

The Western Grain Stabilization Act was designed to stabilize net cash flow from seven major grains and oilseeds produced in the West. It has served that purpose quite well. However, in recent times increased grain marketings have tended to mask the fact that grain prices have fallen and production costs have risen. The program must be made more responsive to the actual financial situation of western grain farmers, and that is what the Government is proposing to do.
When, when?

Another recent federal initiative to assist western farmers was the contribution of $10 million to the Protein Oil Starch Pilot Plant Corporation in Saskatoon. The POS Pilot Plant Corporation conducts research and development work with a view to developing new products and processes with respect to grains and oilseeds. POS is a joint federal Government-industry initiative. This recent contribution is intended to assist it over the next five-year period and to enable it, in conjunction with its industry clientele, to continue to develop a commercial base of operations.
There are many other positive initiatives and contributions which the federal Government has made to the grain and oilseed industry over the years. These are too numerous to mention here since I have only a few minutes remaining. The performance of the Canadian grain industry in exporting grain is one that is unmatched by any other industry and commodity in Canada.
Seven years ago the Canadian Wheat Board proposed an export target of 30 million tonnes of grain by 1985. Exports of grain and products in the 1982-83 crop year reached 29.5 million tonnes, just shy of the 30 million tonne target with two years still to go. I am confident we will achieve and surpass that target with a level of market returns to the producer which would not be possible with any other type of marketing system.
The Government has a good record with respect to recognizing the importance of the Canadian agricultural industry in general, and the western grain industry in particular. I believe the motion of the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette is not well founded. He talks about government inaction. I have demonstrated, as have the Minister and other speakers before me, that we are a government with positive action for the agricultural sector of the economy.
He talked also about government neglect in his motion. If he researches carefully, he will see that we are a government which is sincere about the agricultural industry. We have great respect for the producers of this land. The philosophy of the Liberal Party is to care for all Canadians, to look after all sectors of the economy. It is not to pit one sector against another, one region against another, one Canadian against another, as the Tories like to do.
What a bunch of garbage. We will send you home in a hopper car.

That is what the Tories like to do. They like to disunite the country, yet talk about Canadian unity. They talk bull on their Opposition day. It is the Party of against, of contras, of pitting one region of Canada against another and one sector of the economy against another. They talked about the aerospace industry. What does that industry have to do with the motion before the House? They pitted farmers against the aerospace industry. They should be ashamed of themselves.
April 13, 1984
